tei:titleStmt.tei:title: כַּפָּרוֹת
Kaparōt (using money dedicated for charity), the ritual for the expiation of offenses before Yom Kippur

tei:div.tei:head: Kaparōt (using money dedicated for charity), the ritual for the expiation of offenses before Yom Kippur

tei:l.tei:note: It is customary to observe the custom of Kaparot early in the morning on the eve of Yom Kippur or earlier on the Ten Days of Repentance.
Hold the money of the Kaparot in your right (or dominant) hand and say:

tei:lg.tei:l: Children of Adam —
Some lived in deepest darkness,
bound in cruel irons (Psalms 107:10)
[Hashem] brought them out of deepest darkness,
broke their bonds asunder. (Psalms 107:14)
There were fools who suffered for their sinful way,
and for their iniquities.
All food was loathsome to them;
they reached the gates of death.
In their adversity they cried to YHVH
and [Hashem] saved them from their troubles.
[Hashem] gave an order and healed them;
[Hashem] delivered them from the [charnel] pits.
Let them praise YHVH for [Hashem’s] steadfast love,
the wondrous deeds of [Hashem] for the children of Adam. (Psalms 107:17-21)
If one has a malakh (angelic representative),
[even] one advocate out of a thousand
to declare the person’s uprightness,
then [El] has mercy on them and decrees,
“Redeem them from descending to the [charnel] Pit,
for I have obtained their ransom.” (Job 33:23-24)

tei:l.tei:note: Turn the money over your head three times and say:

tei:lg.tei:l: This is my exchange.
This is my substitute.
This is my expiation.
This money shall be given for tsedaqah
and I will go on to a good long life and to peace.

tei:l.tei:note: Say this entire prayer three times.

Among the Jews of Germany there are those who do not usually turn the Kaparot over their heads but rather bundle the money and place it on a table, place their hand on the bundle and say “this is my Kaparah.” The money of the Kaparot is given to tsedaqah (charity).
